en.content:
HK Electric’s decision to raise its fuel surcharge by 33.9% from July, citing the “deferred effect” of the Middle East conflict, is a reminder that Hong Kong’s day-to-day cost of living remains exposed to forces far beyond the city’s control. Even if the mechanism is financially technical, the impact is immediate: electricity bills will climb, squeezing households that already feel stretched by rent, groceries and other essentials. In this sense, the surcharge is not merely a line item—it is a social pressure test on public trust in utilities and on the wider promise of economic resilience.

That said, transparency matters. When fuel surcharge adjustments are justified with international events, the public is entitled to clear explanations of (1) what exactly drove the higher fuel costs, (2) how “deferred effect” is calculated, and (3) whether any risks are being shared fairly between the utility and consumers. A credible approach would include publishing more granular assumptions—such as fuel price benchmarks and timing—so residents can see whether the increase tracks actual costs rather than simply reflects a lag. For an administration that emphasises stable governance and orderly market operations, better disclosure is also a form of stability: it reduces uncertainty and prevents speculation from filling the gap.

Beyond the accounting, the larger policy question is how Hong Kong prepares for future shocks. The city’s energy transition goals are often framed as long-term environmental work, but reliability and affordability are equally long-term objectives. Even incremental measures—such as improving energy efficiency in the built environment, accelerating grid upgrades, and strengthening demand-side management—can blunt the effect of global volatility on local bills. At the same time, the government and the power sector should review whether the current surcharge framework gives residents adequate predictability. When external crises reverberate through household payments, predictability becomes a public good.

None of this requires undermining the utility’s operational realities; rather, it calls for a balanced contract between service providers and the public. In Hong Kong’s governance context, where consensus and continuity are valued, the key is to ensure that when global events cause costs to rise, the city responds with clarity, efficiency and measured risk-sharing. If transparency improves and resilience measures deepen, the surcharge may still be painful—but it can be understood, and therefore more readily accepted, as part of a disciplined effort to keep electricity dependable in an uncertain world.
en.topic_title: HK Electric to hike fuel surcharge by 33.9% from July over ‘deferred effect’ of war in Middle East

zh.content:
本港電費議題，再一次以「燃料附加費」形式走上檯面。港燈（或中電）在今年7月將燃料附加費上調33.9%，理由係「中東戰事」影響屬延遲效應；表面係宏觀地緣政治傳導，實情卻係市民直接承擔嘅成本壓力。喺物價仍然唔算輕鬆嘅環境下，任何上調都會被大眾解讀為「風險外判」：油價波動由國際市場發酵，再透過本地收費機制落到家庭同小商戶身上。

但社評亦唔應只停留喺「加價就係唔啱」。重點係政府同電力公司應該公開交代，咁大幅度嘅上調係基於乜嘢量化指標、對應咩成本項目、以及有冇可控空間。燃料附加費長期以「公式」運作，若公式只提供結果、卻缺乏足夠透明度，就容易變成市民對決策流程失去信任。更重要嘅係，喺本港要提升能源韌性、同推動更清潔能源嘅方向之下，燃料附加費就唔可以永遠當作「被動調整」——應該同步講清楚：中短期如何分散風險、長期如何降低對單一燃料同單一地緣事件嘅依賴。

另一方面，地緣政治風險確實存在，亦真係會影響能源供應同價格；紛爭唔只屬於新聞頭條，而係會反映到實際成本。正因如此，政府更應該扮演「監督同對沖」角色：一方面要確保成本核算可信，另一方面亦要檢視資費機制能否兼顧效率與公平——例如針對低收入家庭、長者同基層商戶，是否有更精準、可預期嘅支援安排，而唔係每次成本上升都由社會普遍吸收。

總結而言，33.9%唔係一個抽象百分比，而係街坊日常生活嘅算術題。社會可以理解外部衝擊，但更需要看到本地制度對衝擊嘅回應：透明嘅成本拆解、清晰嘅風險管理、同對弱勢更具可及性嘅支援。只有咁，市民先至願意相信每一次資費調整，都唔係單向加壓，而係在可控範圍內合理承擔、並持續改善。
